catalog_quote: As palavras dissilábicas não parecem ter acento fixo, de modo que é possível encontrar palavras desse tipo sendo acentuadas ora na última, ora na penúltima sílaba, da direita para a esquerda. [...] Nas palavras trissilábicas e polissilábicas, por sua vez, o acento parece ser fixo, uma vez que recai sempre na penúltima sílaba das palavras [p. 153] [...] É importante enfatizar ainda, no que se refere ao acento em Mehináku, que existem alguns contextos que parecem favorecer o deslocamento do acento na língua. Esses contextos, em geral, são aqueles de juntura morfológica, em especial na sufixação, em que morfemas são acrescentados à direita dos itens verbais ou nominais. [p. 154] [...] Os sufixos do tipo {=nau}; {=tai}; {=pai} e outros com estrutura CVV, por sua vez, formam um núcleo complexo, sendo, portanto, compreendidos como sílabas pesadas, razão pela qual tendem a atrair o acento (HAYES, 1995). Além disso, dado o processo de sufixação, é possível propor, a priori, que o acento tende a deslocar-se proeminentemente à direita em Mehináku, o que parece indicar a preferência da língua por um padrão troqueu. [p. 156] [...] O acento geralmente não é contrastivo. [p. 70]

new_statements.quote: As palavras dissilábicas não parecem ter acento fixo, de modo que é possível encontrar palavras desse tipo sendo acentuadas ora na última, ora na penúltima sílaba, da direita para a esquerda. [...] Nas palavras trissilábicas e polissilábicas, por sua vez, o acento parece ser fixo, uma vez que recai sempre na penúltima sílaba das palavras [...] (p. 153). É importante enfatizar ainda, no que se refere ao acento em Mehináku, que existem alguns contextos que parecem favorecer o deslocamento do acento na língua. Esses contextos, em geral, são aqueles de juntura morfológica, em especial na sufixação (p. 154). [p. 70:] O acento geralmente não é contrastivo.
new_statements.translation: Disyllabic words do not seem to have fixed stress, so that words of this type can be found stressed now on the last, now on the penultimate syllable, counting from right to left. [...] In trisyllabic and polysyllabic words, in turn, stress seems to be fixed, since it always falls on the penultimate syllable of the word (p. 153). It is important to stress further, regarding stress in Mehináku, that there are some contexts that seem to favour stress displacement in the language. These contexts are generally those of morphological juncture, especially suffixation (p. 154). [p. 70:] Stress is generally not contrastive.
new_statements.citation: de Felipe, Paulo Henrique Pereira Silva. 2020. Fonologia e morfossintaxe da língua Mehináku (Arawak). PhD thesis, Universidade Estadual de Campinas, Instituto de Estudos da Linguagem. §2.7 'Acento', pp. 152-156.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened (504 pp., text, printed page = PDF page). §2.7 'Acento' heading is on p. 152 (TOC also says 152); the quoted sentences are verbatim on p. 153 ('As palavras dissilábicas não parecem ter acento fixo, de modo que é possível encontrar palavras desse tipo sendo acentuadas ora na última, ora na penúltima sílaba, da direita para a esquerda' and 'Nas palavras trissilábicas e polissilábicas, por sua vez, o acento parece ser fixo, uma vez que recai sempre na penúltima sílaba das palavras'), the displacement sentence is verbatim on p. 154, 'O acento geralmente não é contrastivo' is verbatim on p. 70 (§1.5 Perfil linguístico), and the summary on p. 471 repeats the rule ('as palavras dissilábicas…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words of three or more syllables are stressed on the penult without exception in the author's data (a.ˈmɨ.ɲa 'cold', ka.tu.pa.ˈlu.lu 'widow'); disyllables are lexically either final (pa.ˈpa 'father', ʂe.ˈpi 'bench') or penult (ˈu.nɨ 'water', ˈte.me 'tapir'); monosyllables of shape VV/CVV bear prominence on the first vowel (falling diphthong). Adding a CV.CV suffix to a disyllable yields penult stress on the suffix's first syllable (itsa-ˈtɨpe 'canoes'); CVV suffixes/enclitics (=nau, =tai, =pai) are treated as heavy and take the stress themselves (tɨneʐu=ˈnau 'women', n=aĩtʃa=ˈpai 'I am eating'). The author reads the rightward drift as a preference for a trochaic pattern. In the earlier 2018 SETA paper (pp. 118-120) he had instead derived disyllabic final stress from syllable weight (final when both syllables light, penult when the first has a long vowel), an account the thesis no longer uses.
new_statements.exceptions: Disyllables are split between oxytone and paroxytone with no rule given (lexical). Monosyllabic demonstrative ʂa is unstressed in sentences. Proclitics and enclitics never bear stress (pp. 197-200), yet the CVV enclitics =nau, =tai, =pai attract stress when attached (pp. 154-156). Inalienable nouns with final stress shift to penult stress when possessed (kiˈri 'nose' vs nu=ˈkiri 'my nose', p. 213). Final stress on a noun can signal nominalization (p. 178).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (roots plus suffixes and enclitics), citation forms elicited by the author; 'geralmente não é contrastivo' is stated at the word level. No phrase-level statement.
new_statements.identity_note: de Felipe 2020 describes the Mehináku of the Xingu Indigenous Territory (Aikhenvald's Paresi-Xingu branch, Xingu subgroup), ca. 325 speakers, i.e. mehi1240 itself; no dialect split is invoked. Note the two competing analyses of disyllables by the same author (weight-based in de Felipe 2018 SETA pp. 118-120; lexical/unfixed in the 2020 thesis p. 153).

new_statements.translation: The non-possessed form can equally be indicated by changes in the position of the stress, or by vowel changes accompanied by vowel harmony. [p. 253] || 1) Presence of the suffix {-i} and a shift of the stress from the penultimate syllable of the possessed noun to the last syllable of the root, in the absolute form, as in (16). [...] 3) Shift of the stressed penultimate syllable of the possessed form to the final syllable in the non-possessed form [p. 254] || Moreover, the penultimate syllable of the word in the possessive structure is stressed, as in the following data. [p. 255] || In this type of construction there is a change in the position of the stressed syllable, from the penult, which characterises the non-possessed form, to the final position of the word in the possessed structure, as seen in (22). new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with de Felipe 2020 (penultimate in words of 3+ syllables, suffixes attract stress, stress generally non-contrastive): Corbera Mori 2007 also has penult as the default and shows the same mobility, but adds that the shift between penult and final stress is exploited morphologically to distinguish possessed from absolute (non-possessed) nouns. The disyllabic pairs with final stress in absolute or possessed forms (ki'yi, nu-pala'ta) are the kind of variation de Felipe 2020 reports for disyllables. It is not a contradiction: the catalog's penult reading stands, with a morphological-conditioning refinement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general stress rule is stated (the paper is on nominal morphology, not phonology). What it says: in possessed inalienable nouns and in alienable nouns carrying the possessive suffix -la/-le/-ja/-ya the penult is stressed; the penult is also the stressed syllable of unpossessed alienable nouns. Stress position is then used as a morphological marker: absolute (non-possessed) forms of inalienables move stress to the root-final / word-final syllable (with -i, or with a final vowel change to -i, or with no segmental change, e.g. nu-'kiyi 'my nose' vs ki'yi 'nose'), and a lexically conditioned set of alienables moves stress from penult to final when possessed (pa'lata 'comb' vs nu-pala'ta). So: penultimate default, with morphologically conditioned final stress.
new_statements.exceptions: Stress shift as a morphological exponent: (a) absolute/non-possessed forms of inalienable nouns take root-final or word-final stress (examples 16-18, p. 254; e.g. kana'ti 'mouth' vs nu-ka'nati 'my mouth'); (b) a lexically conditioned set of alienable nouns takes final stress when possessed (§3.3, examples 22, p. 256); (c) in §3.2 a final vowel that nasalises in the possessed form also becomes stressed (p. 256). Kinship terms have irregular paradigms (p. 255).
new_statements.identity_note: Corbera Mori 2007 describes data collected from speakers of the Utawana village on the rio Kurisevo (Xingu Indigenous Park, Mato Grosso); the paper notes that Waurá and Mehináku speakers are mutually intelligible but the two languages differ in lexicon and phonetics-phonology. No other dialect is described.

sources.note: §2.7 'Acento' pp. 152-156: disyllables have no fixed stress (either final or penult, lexically); trisyllables and longer words always stressed on the penult; certain suffixes/enclitics (=nau, -tɨpe, -pɨhɨ, =tai, -taɾi, =taku, -pɨku, =pai) attract stress rightward, heavy CVV suffixes take it themselves; p. 70: stress 'geralmente não é contrastivo'; clitics unstressed (pp. 197-200); possession can shift final stress to penult in inalienable nouns (p. 213).

sources.note: §3 'O acento em Mehináku' pp. 118-120: earlier, weight-based analysis of disyllables — final stress when both syllables are light, penult when the first syllable is heavy (long vowel); trisyllables and longer always penult; concludes the system is 'free' for disyllables and fixed for longer words. Superseded by the 2020 thesis, which drops the vowel-length account.
